Unfortunately a 6.5/10 for me at the moment. Core elements remain the same as in previous iterations, but new mechanics are implemented very poorly and detract from the overall experience. Most notably, the developers added vertical movement (a la Assassin's Creed), but--unlike in AC--while you can climb *some* surfaces such as vines, you can't even walk up the bank of a road or hop over a small pile of rocks. This leads to extremely awkward gameplay where you are never sure whether you can climb over something or not (usually not), and have to try first to find out.

The aforementioned problem also means that the large open map, another new feature, is actually not large at all. For example, there are some roads that you simply cannot walk off of because you are somehow unable to ascend a 15 degree incline, despite being able to climb the side of a house. Compounding this problem are barriers that have absolutely no reason to be barriers, such as slightly-dense foliage and low walls. Why can I climb over medium walls but not low walls?

The worst is when you find out you can actually climb something, such as as a side of a house--only to realize that it leads to a dead end (i.e. you cannot top out) and your only option is to climb back down. Remove the ambiguity, please.

The redeeming quality is that, once you get past the fence that could only be cut in one place but not another, and actually get sniping, it's the same old goodness as before.

The new 'invasion' mechanic is implemented horribly.  I don't know who worked on it, but it suddenly expects you to play like you're in some battle royale arena instead of Sniper Elite.  I was invaded in the first level, died because I tried to be aggressive, and was immediately invaded again, so I decided to find a defensible location and watch my angles of approach (y'know, like a sniper, in my sniping game) but was immediately penalised for 'camping' by having my location revealed.

It wouldn't be so bad if there was some incentive to approach each other over time, but with open maps the size of some small countries, no time limit, and no regular hints about where the other guy is hiding (unless you use telephones, which can be booby-trapped), dealing with a single invader can take upwards of ten minutes.  And this, in turn, wouldn't be such a big deal either, if you didn't get XP docked for playing with invasions disabled.

If Rebellion is so proud of this new "feature" that they'll punish you for opting out, you'd think they'd have made sure to iron out the kinks first.  I'll review this game properly if they find some way to make the invasions fun, or stop punishing people who opt out, because right now, they're a stain on the whole experience.

[h2]Sniper Elite 5 Review[/h2]
	
[h2]Storyline[/h2]
I am pretty sure you would have realized that the Sniper Elite series are gameplay-heavy games. In Layman’s terms, the Sniper Elite series is known for the Genre-specific gameplay rather than the storylines. People play this game just to attain satisfaction from the kill cams or for the fun co-op experience they offer. 

There is a lot of redundancy in the storyline across the series. It usually involves infiltrating bases, taking out the higher-ups, and finally killing Adolf Hitler. The games’ plots are always something along these lines. So, if you’re looking for a proper unique storyline in this game, this isn’t meant for you. Let me sum up the entire plot in one line:

[code]Play again as Karl Fairburne in 1944 France as he fights to uncover a secret Nazi project called Project Kraken.[/code]

Yeah yeah, it’s the same ol’ plot. Karl is immortal or some shit & Hitler can apparently respawn. Alright, I’ll stop questioning the logic in this game’s story.

[h2]Gameplay Mechanics[/h2]
The gameplay part of the game is what made this series so popular. The kill cams and the gory after-effects of your shots are what the players find most appealing. Well, here are the multiple segments again:

[b][u]Core Gameplay[/u][/b]
The core gameplay remains the same. As I mentioned in the introduction, Sniper Elite has established a solid gameplay. It’s already challenging and fun. It is because of this that the developers are not trying to introduce any major differences whenever they release a new part. And the good thing is, people are barely complaining. 

So, each mission takes place in an open-worldish environment where you are given multiple objectives. Yeah, the objectives are very similar to the ones from the previous games; killing targets, destroying stuff, etc. The very generic shooter game objectives. What’s good is that you are given completely free reign on how you approach these tasks. There’s no laid path for you to follow to complete the missions. Since it’s an open-world setting, you get to choose your own approach; stealth or guns blazing. I prefer stealth since that’s how a sniper should actually take down their targets. At the same time, I take up the guns-blazing approach when I run thin on patience. 

You must be wondering how one would take a guns-blazing approach in a Sniper-focused game. Well, you have secondary weapons. These secondary weapons obviously have less ammo to discourage relying on them all the time. It’s best to use them when you’re in a pinch or want to take out someone in close range!

[b][u]So, What’s New?[/u][/b]
Apart from the usual upgrades to the already existing features, Rebellion apparently added a handful of new features to Sniper Elite 5. So, here is the list of the so-called new features:
[olist]
[*] [b]Improvements to the game’s campaign:[/b] They’ve taken references from real places and included them in the game now. Some assets used are the result of photogrammetry which gives them more detail since they are basically scans of real objects. You can now share ammunition and healing items with your co-op partner. 
[*] [b]Weapon customization and Map Traversal:[/b] Weapon customization has become a bit more detailed by allowing you to customize almost every part of the weapon. Traveling across the map has been enhanced a bit through the addition of slopes and ziplines which can come in handy in various situations.
[*] [b]Invasion Mode:[/b] This is an entirely new campaign-based PvP mode they introduced in this part. This allows randoms to invade your playthrough. Their main target is taking you out. This adds a bit more spice to your playthrough while making it a bit more challenging. 
[*] [b]An Enhanced Killcam:[/b] The Killcam in the Sniper Elite series has been one of the most vital features the game offers. They keep on making it better and better with every new release. So, it’s pretty obvious that they have made a lot of improvements to the kill cam in this game. It’s more graphic than ever!
[/olist]
[i]Source: [url=https://gamerant.com/sniper-elite-5-improvements-campaign-weapons-traversal/#:~:text=Sniper%20Elite%205%20will%20additionally,companion%20within%20co%2Doperative%20gameplay.]Gamerant Website on the Same Topic.[/url][/i]

So yeah, this is all the new stuff the game offers. Not a lot but the core gameplay is what would keep you hooked. And yes, I had to look up the stuff that was new in this game since they were not very obvious when I played the game. I hope the next part will have actual noticeable introductions.

[b][u]Difficulty Modes[/u][/b]
So, there’s a new difficulty mode in Sniper Elite V named “Civilian”. It’s now the easiest mode. The other difficulty modes are the same as they were in the previous parts:
[olist]
[*] [b]Civilian:[/b] As the name suggests, pretend that a civilian is given a Sniper Elite and is thrown into the battlefield. The civilian would now know how to fend for themselves. Hence, everything should be easy as fuck in order for the civilian to have higher odds of surviving. That’s basically this mode, easy as fuck.
[*] [b]Cadet:[/b] This is the somewhat easy mode where weapon ballistic is omitted and the AI would have the IQ of a rock. 
[*] [b]Sharpshooter:[/b] Basically, a slightly harder difficulty mode where bullet drop is a thing. Enemies can now aim a bit better and can deal a bit more damage to you.
[*] [b]Sniper Elite:[/b] Oh my god! This difficulty mode is the name of the game! But it isn’t the hardest difficulty mode. This is where the actual sniper ballistics come into play. You have no assistance whatsoever. Everything becomes manual.
[*] [b]Authentic:[/b] The hardest mode the game has to offer. As the name states, this mode is as hard as real-life….apparently. It requires a lot of skill since enemies are as sharp as a knife and can deal a shit tonne of damage to you. Pretty sure they can one-shot you.
[/olist]

Apart from these, there’s obviously a custom difficulty mode where you can alter the difficulty of the different aspects of the game. These options not only make the game tailor-made for you but also add a lot to the replayability rate. 

[h2]Visuals & Audio[/h2]

The visuals have greatly improved when compared to its predecessor. Everything is way more detailed and polished right now. I love the new gorey and overly-detailed kill cam kills. It’s way more satisfying! The visuals are an easy 10/10! As for the audio part of the game, I am not really sure what to say since I didn’t pay that much attention to it. I was a bit too focused on the gameplay…

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[list]
[*] The killcam still reigns supreme.
[*] You have complete freedom on how you want to approach a mission.
[*] The AI is challenging depending on your chosen difficulty mode.
[*] There’s quite a handful of difficulty modes to choose from which adds a bit to the game’s variety and replayability rate.
[/list]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[list]
[*] The story is very dull and kinda repetitive since the previous games have a similar plot.
[*] The missions also feel repetitive.
[*] There are minor bugs but I am sure the developers will rectify them in the upcoming updates!
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Sniper Elite games always manage to fascinate me. I am a sucker for the kill cams and the authentic sniper mechanics. Yeah, the game is a bit too pricey. It is worth that price but I do recommend waiting for a sale. It’s very expensive since it might be considered a AAA Release. If you wait long enough, I am sure the game would go for a dirt-cheap price!

Despite bearing the name of previous Sniper Elite games, this is not a game about sniping, but about tactical warfare. The levels seem open, but force you via certain routes, and the enemy AI will rush your position as soon as they hear a single shot. This game was best played by choosing a position behind a choke point, and luring the enemy in via the above mentioned mechanics, and taking them down using an SMG.

The choice of weapons is disappointing, as are the (unrealistic) modifications. Almost all shooting happens at close range (<50m~150m). The storyine, which is for most part a bad ripoff from sniper elite 4, is extremely boring, with predictable and bland punchlines, and it lacks the suspense which was found in the previous installments. The acting within the game is cringy, but apart from that, not really noteworthy, since there is little to none to be found.

But above all, this game departs from the traditional sniping base, in a way I hope Rebellion will recover from.

It pains me to write this review, because I loved the previous game dearly, and while I certainly don't hate this iteration, I'm just... disappointed. Short version: this game is one step forward, 15 small steps back.

Longer version - Oh boy, let me list you my grievances:
- Our protagonist appears to have been dropped on his head between games, and while he still remembers how to pick up guns from fallen enemies, he is entirely incapable of conceiving of how to reload them, and will instead simply discard them once the initial ammo runs out. Or any time you switch weapon, for that matter.
- Speaking of weapons, the initial selection (including unlockables) is a travesty, with basically every well-known rifle from the period suspiciously missing from the list (which is made up of a lackluster 6 rifles of mostly obscure models... almost like someone was planning to sell back the fan favourites as DLC down the line. Almost.)
- Then there's the elephant in the room - invasion mode. To be fair here, I am in no way protesting its existence, and I wish anyone excited by it a jolly good time - but to have singleplayer PvE unlockables gated to not only participation, but performance in a PvP mode, that's gonna be a hard yikes from me. Insult to injury that turning it off results in a penalty to all xp earned.
- Along with reloading enemy weapons, our protag has also forgotten how to pick up rocks from the ground for easy throwing, and must now rely entirely on whatever glass bottles he can find along the way.
- (As a trade-off, he appears to have learned to harness his latent psychic abilities in order to sense enemies through walls. YMMW on this one)
- Your mileage may also vary on the gun customization feature. While it's not COD-levels of bad, it's certainly taking some historical liberties - and every single attachment available somehow make some aspect of the gun worse, a design decision I personally loathe.
- Traversing is great, until it ain't. When it works, traversal feels... very decent. But there's a lot of times where there are no visual cues and even less logic to what you can and can't climb, and at least the first map is plagued by knee-high impassable obstacles, invisible walls, and long stretches of ditches, vegetation or fencing that any normal human should be able to traverse with ease, but our protag inexplicably cannot.
- Finally, there's a lot of things that, while not outright bad, also just aren't as good as they were before. Tagged enemies don't show up as they used to, making visibility sometimes an issue. Empty lung looks and feels just a little worse than before (in part because it now has a wind-up time of sorts, making repeat shots less fluid). The kill-cams, while now available from just about any weapon (which is great) just look... jankier, somehow - which is kindof impressive, to be honest.

All in all - it's hard not to come across as someone with a vendetta writing this, but I feel it is an accurate representation of the game in it's current state. It's not that the game is not fun, and I definitely plan on putting more hours in it - but I've already paid for it, and I'd be lying if I said I wasn't disappointed. I feel overall let down with some of the choices made by the design team. I'm sure a lot of this will change and improve with patches and DLC, but in its current state, I really cannot think of a reason to recommend anyone buy this over Sniper Elite 4.

[h1]First time into Sniper Elite series[/h1]

You can't see there are different ways to reach the objectives at first---you only figure it out after disastrous attempts. Then the real fun starts.

Getting creative rewards as the game progresses. While I tend to sneak and wait---the singleplayer campaign can be played in 4 styles; from "non-lethal" (no kills), to "lethal" which can be noisy. I have an impatient friend that usually plays Rambo; that's the 3rd style, "assault." 

To get your style better, you can evolve Karl's skills into three segments: combat, equipment and body. Can also equip or man temporary guns or mod yours in workbenches.

Moving like a shadow I land in the 4th style: "stealth," but since class can combine, I'm also fall into lethal. If I have to blow a bunker because the silent option is FUBAR, I'd bobby-trap possible reinforcement routes or sabotage proxy installations. Can wait for external sounds to pull the trigger and mask the boom. 

Sometimes I'm non-lethal to avoid alarming the scorn about my presence, even though blowing fascists into smithereens is very tempting.

Campaign story is ok but cutscenes are just generic body-capture. Maybe fans of the series still want to know about whatever happened to their characters. The only thing I know is that you'd be working behind France's liberation via Atlantic Wall behind of the lines, providing covert-ops---quite like Splinter Cell used to do. Game is unusually doing that in the 40s era.

Voice acting is formidable though. Main character Karl is voiced by Tom Clarke Hill (from Tony the tiger cornflakes), and the man is very good at it. Lois Chimimba voices Charlie, instantly removing the boring cliche of "damsel" straight to a bad-ass girl. The list goes.

There is a co-op mode (it's more fun with friends), counter-coop or player invasion (if you allow it) and there is a survival mode and classic multiplayer. Expect a lot of DLC trying to cash-in after your buy, but none are really that needed unless you want to extend the game's shelve life and play some more.

Eg; when you bobby-trap something, the camera makes sure to show you if some fascist tripped on it, but limbs won't be mutilated. If cams breaks your immersion then just turn it off.

The constant pop-up on the HUD whenever I shoot pigs in a special way can be annoying. It's like arcade when hitting high-scores. That might work for multiplayer fun galore, but not when you're immersed in singleplayer. At least you can deactivate some of it with difficulty options.

I nicknamed gaming as "outward" and "inward" to define the world focus when reviewing Watch Dogs 2 years ago.

Games like Tomb Raider 2013 got attention to details closer to a center, so the world might look harder to reach and the main character more detailed. That's the "inward" type.

The "outward" types are usually games wider to the sides. They tend to lose details around the character, focusing in the open world and making it lighter. Some games mixes both, such as GTA V that leans more to outward than GTA IV so the world was a bit easier to reach. RDR2 is the only one that had the guts to mix extremes, mega detailed and inward in a wide open world.

I expected Sniper Elite 5 to have limitations---devs are an independent company. But I also expected it to be a lot more heavy and inward. Funny enough, it is not.

Attention to details are not satisfying where it should, you don't see anything deeper as the game looks to be. One example: you crawl into bushes and mud for hours, but still come out clean, looking hot and with great hair.

I avoided buying this for a long time because I'd heard horror stories about respawning enemies ruining the usual gameplay loop of level-clearing - and of invasions meaning you'd get griefed all the time.

I finally grabbed it on this Autumn Sale and... neither of those things is true. I've yet to encounter a respawned enemy (that I noticed), and Invasions default to 'off'.

This is just more Sniper Elite 4, but a bit prettier. 

The pricing and DLC structure is still a dark-pattern horror-show... but it isn't a bad game at all, it delivers exactly what I loved about the previous installments.

This game is a fantastic successor to Sniper Elite 4 and adds new features that fit right in with the franchise. They’ve improved the formula in almost every way, but didn’t compromise the core identity of the game. Rebellion understands the phrase, “If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it” and in the era of modern gaming, this is fantastic. And hey, if you’re just looking for a fun new action stealth game and haven’t touched a Sniper Elite game in your life, I highly recommend this to you too.

The core gameplay is incredibly strong. It feels well put together and satisfying to play. The game’s movement and weapon handling feels more tactile and immersive than ever before, especially with the new active reload system. The weapons feel punchy and the gunshots are very satisfying. The AI is a bit more dynamic this time around but it’s nothing to write home about, it’s stealth game AI. They can’t be perfectly smart even on the hardest difficulties or else the game wouldn’t be fun (This is why Invasion Mode is so fun. More on that later). The game also provides you with tons of different playstyles all equally viable, and with the addition of a graph summarizing your playstyle upon the end of the mission, it ups the replay value and feels fun to try different methods. If you’re a completionist, this game will give you something to chew on for a while with lots of collectibles, badges and achievements.

The actual narrative of the campaign is a bit different than other SE titles in that it actually tries to tell a bit of a story. It’s still mostly just “World War 2 people, doing World War 2 stuff.” But the characters are a little more memorable and there is a narrative that shines through. It’s not why you play the game, but it’s there. Just a way to provide reasons for why you’re playing through the missions that you are. It’s not bad, because it never tries to be good. Rebellion knows exactly what they’re trying to make and I respect that. It’s like John Wick, or Nobody. There doesn’t always need to be an incredible narrative, sometimes you can just have fun.

There are some cool gameplay features new to Sniper Elite that fit the formula pretty naturally. You can now pick up enemy weapons WITHOUT replacing what’s in your loadout, in the form of a “temporary weapon” that is dropped when empty, or unloaded manually for its ammo, meaning there’s a LOT more ammo to go around for your loadout weapons. You can now toggle between soft aim and aim down sights with any weapon, even SMGs and handguns. There’s nonlethal options now! I’m not a huge fan of the fact that sparing the nazis you’ve been sent to kill gives a huge XP bonus, I usually just wished I were able to spare one or two guys that I read about on the binoculars, not play a pacifist SOE commando behind enemy lines. But more optional gameplay styles are no skin off my back, always welcome, glad it doesn’t affect how I want to play. There’s also a more in depth customization system than Sniper Elite has ever had, with so many stats for each weapon it makes your head hurt. You can look more into the stats, or look at a simple visual summary if you don’t care. All the attachments available can start teetering on “cursed gun” territory like CoD Vanguard but nothing that’s unforgivable or COMPLETELY immersion breaking.

The multiplayer aspects of this game are cool, the deathmatch, free for all and objective modes are fun enough, they’re what you’d expect. It’s Sniper Elite but PvP. I haven’t sunk much time into these modes, but the time I have spent was very fun, it’s just not the thing I’m looking for when I boot up SE. When I do, it’s because I want fun stealth and cool killcams, but if you like the idea of sniper deathmatch, go nuts! There’s also Co-Op survival and campaign. Co-Op campaign seems a blast, I love Co-Op stealth experiences, but I don’t have any friends that play, and I haven’t felt the need to delve into Discord or Steam communities to find playmates. Survival seems to have gotten a bit of a downgrade in terms of map count and possibly map size as well, compared to SE4. It also feels much harder. Some command posts feel near impossible to defend from there just being no safe vantage points or high ground and there being way too many flank routes to viably defend against. Aside from a few QoL improvements to the survival formula, I prefer the experience of previous survival iterations more. Give us more maps, guys! Now, all other multiplayer aside, Rebellion has done something fabulous with this one:

There is now, of course, Invasion mode. Invade a player’s campaign mission and hunt them down as an Axis Sniper. That is so damn cool. It’s like the sniper boss fight in Metal Gear Solid, at its best. A tense matchup of two equals, a dangerous game of cat and mouse. At its worst, it’s a game of chicken where the other player finds your approximate location, and bum-rushes you with an SMG. But even then, it’s over quickly and you can get back to finding a good matchup! It’s usually an incredibly fun experience. I can’t figure out which side I like to play more. This may be my favorite mode. I’ve gotten over 100 kills now as the invader and something over two dozen kills as the invaded. Each has their own advantages and disadvantages. I highly recommend the campaign with Invasion on. Getting invaded by a thinking enemy when you’d otherwise breeze through the mission of hapless minions immediately changes the tone to something much more intense. Especially when that enemy can put on the exact same uniform as any other NPC and walk around slowly in a group with them, blending in near perfectly (This is still my favorite way to play as the Jaeger, even with the ghillie suit an option for me now).

Last but certainly not least is killcams. ALL weapons now feature killcams. Handguns, rifles and SMGs. It’s cool, I always wanted the option for other guns to have them. Cool cinematic trickshots shouldn’t be limited to just rifles! And like SE4, melee kills, traps and explosions all feature killcams now as well. There is so much more detail in the X-Ray models it’s almost too much, to the point of taking away from other details. It’s certainly gross and seems anatomically correct, but do I need to see like, the salivary glands in the jaw? It obscures the destruction physics on the bones! I digress. The boring, repetitive organ shots of SE4 have been improved. It used to be that any time there was a fatal shot on an organ, say a liver, that it would BLUR OUT all the other amazingly detailed layers (muscle, bone, etc.) and just focus on a hi-def render of a floating liver getting split in half, the same way, every time. But they’ve done away with this now! The frequency of this has been decreased, and the organs all dynamically respond to the caliber of the bullet that hit, and the direction it hit from. There are also bullet hole effects on enemies now, making X-Ray free killcams very brutal, and still immersive. Used to be that the ai would make a ridiculous face as a floating bullet phased through their nose, with no blood in sight. But no more! It’s a little lazy, just adding a generic blood spat on the exit wound. But when it covers a textured part of the body like the eye socket, it really looks like you blew the dude’s face off. When the blood effect is just pasted onto a flat surface, like the bald head of an enemy, or a torso, it looks pretty boring. And why oh why aren’t there destruction physics on the character models themselves? There’s a beautifully dynamic, fully destructible skeletal system, but if I blow a jaw off in the X-Ray, the guy’s chin is beautifully intact!! Anyway, the killcams have also been improved in every single way, I’m just nitpicking.

In summary this game MIGHT be the best in the franchise but I'd have to replay all to be 100% sure. Like I said, I recommend it to Sniper Elite veterans, shooter fans, and stealth game fans. Definitely a hard cop, maybe even get the DLC too.
The best part of the game is when a wounded Hitler was stammering and pleading for his life only to say "Mein Gott, Karl really is the Sniper Elite 5!"

I wasn’t expecting it to be as good as it is. As a long time Hitman fan, this was superb. I had never played the fourth entry before, though I went through the first three, which were solid but lacked the incredible environmental design found here. Some of these missions have the best layouts I’ve ever played, and the third mission genuinely stunned me. It hooked me the same way Hitman does making me want to revisit each location to explore it more thoroughly, since I usually don’t the first time around. The level layouts make sense, and the scale is absolutely impressive. The freedom to approach objectives in multiple ways really enhances the experience, making each mission unique which was awesome might I add and coming from the third game that surprised me.

The gunplay is excellent the sniping feels impactful, and the iconic kill cam is as satisfying as ever. Its just the medium range that lacks finesse so usually the best option is either close up or long range which suits the game and guns ablazing is possible but not without the right loadout. The ability to customize weapons is always appreciated and my god are there a lot of options available to you, even a testing range to try out your combinations, and you will want to replay missions to unlock new weapons since only a limited amount of armaments are available from the beginning. However, it’s not without flaws. The story is your usual fan fare and characters aren’t particularly strong they mostly serve as background for the gameplay. The AI can be inconsistent, sometimes reacting unrealistically, and there are moments where close quarters combat overshadows the sniping focus. All in all, it’s much better than I expected, and I’d wholeheartedly recommend everyone give it a try especially since it’s often available at a steep discount.

Recommend? Yes, absolutely... but sadly another game tainted by DLC.

Base game = Excellent. Very few complaints. I started dabbling in the SE series starting with the OG and V2 remastered, but really got into it with 3 onward. I would rate this the best among 3, 4 and 5 as far as the which I've enjoyed the most. 5 has most of the good aspects of 4 but with bigger maps with more options of routes and how to approach. Weapon upgrades and attachments are better handled as well as more varied and interesting. Replayability is good too, I've come back on harder difficulty trying different weapon setups and different approaches. I have all gold medals for the core game challenges and I've enjoyed every minute of it.

Where this game falls short is in fact not the actual base game, it's the DLC. I've picked up a few small DLCs that were mostly weapons and skins. These weapons added some ridiculous award requirements that require some truly mind numbing grinding, and for what? This clued me in to Rebellion's tactics, and the more I've read the reviews on subsequent season DLCs, I've decided against spending any money on the additional content. Yes, I would LOVE to have new maps to play... but given the cost they charge and the reviews show clearly the additional maps are not well thought out, it just reeks of DLC cash grab and I'm sick of that from these publishers. Rebellion needs this feedback. Loved your game and happy with my purchase, but will absolutely Not spend additional money on over priced, low quality DLCs. It's not acceptable.

If you like SE4.......

I held off buying SE5 because of negative reviews and the many similar complaints among them. I almost let those negative opinions influence me to pass up this game I am enjoying. Here are some of the common gripes that are just not true......

1) "Not open world". "Game-play is funneled by obstacles". 
NOT TRUE.  The map can be traversed by many ways just as in SE4. Even with hedgerows that are common to north France, I feel no constriction.
2) "Few  opportunities for sniper long shots." "Penalized for remaining in one place too long." 
NOT TRUE. I find many vantage points where I remain undetected that afford plenty of opportunity for those satisfying long shots. But if I remain concealed in place too long near the enemy the AI has increasing chance to spot me. 
3) "Feels less like a sniper game and more like a special ops stealth game" and "Stealth is not done well."
NOT TRUE. SE5 offers both and does both very well. And when time comes to run and gun well placed grenades and sub-machine gun spray provide very exciting game play.

Single player.....
Much is said about multi-play and Invasion mode but I play only single-play. Invasion mode can be toggled off. Solo play through the campaign is very enjoyable.

Replay value....
Campaign maps provide many ways to complete and the enemy AI will challenge in diverse ways resulting in unique play every time. 

I could go on. But you the reader have also seen the objections that have you hesitant like I was to try SE5. So I write this positive review with hope my words will help you decide to give SE5 a try. Be aware of the time spent playing as you test the game for yourself. Do not go over the two hour refund mark. If you do not like SE5 then just refund it. But I know some of you are like me and will discover SE5 to be a very enjoyable experience.

Hmmm. This is NOT a sniping game.  WW2 Sam Fisher wannabe in an environment where a sniper rifle is hardly ever, ever used. Basically redundant. Stealth is the name of this game, and silenced side arm is key.  Which grinds after 14 + hours of play. Dissappointed.

A sniping game designed so that sniping is the least optimal way to complete a mission.
TLDR: The game's focus has changed from picking off targets from 100s of metres away on a vantage point, to melee executions and silenced pistols in close quarters

First of all the massive change in focus from picking enemies off from a tower / rooftop / mountain without compromising your position, to levels mostly designed around close quarters, using stealth executions, silenced pistols for most of the levels where sniping at 20m just isn't fun.

The second major problem is that when there are opportunities for long range sniping, you can only really fire one shot before everything goes loud, since when you shoot your first bullet, everyone within a 200 metre radius goes into full panic mode, and sounds an alarm which spawns reinforcements. If they won't be alerted by the shot, they'll be alerted by the guard being shot.

Now, in previous Sniper Elite games, you avoided that by picking your targets correctly, and it was satisfying completing a whole level without guards ever knowing they were being picked off. Or if they did panic, you could continue sniping them while they lost their minds. Not in this one

The last major problem is the considerably strange objectives for a stealth / sniper game, such as 'use explosives to destroy an AA gun', which automatically alerts all the guards thanks to a giant explosion and their equipment being destroyed?
it took me 5 hours on authentic mode to finish one mission , pray for me.

Fun game sneaking around popping Nazis.
My only complaint is about the invisible walls that stop you going into advantageous  areas. Its gotten me killed a couple of times.  Like you have these large open maps (which I like)great for planning out how you get in &out only to have your emergency run way route blocked by an invisible wall :-/

This game plays smooth, allows the player to tackle levels as they wish, and feels polished. If you like the Sniper Elite formula, you'll probably like this too. Seeing as the game is a few years old at this point, it surely goes on sale often; buy it then. As I write this, its $4.99, which is definitely a steal.

Things I particularly enjoyed include the highest difficulty/immersion game play setting which forced me to actually pay attention without feeling unfair (although you can customize multiple difficulty settings as you wish), gathering all the collectibles which allowed me to thoroughly explore each level (there are enough without feeling bloated), and the scale of each level (and the pacing of the game overall). 

Some things I didn't particularly enjoy was the AA options (too aliased although you might like the crunchy look). Also, at least when I played, there was a memory leak that would gradually fill up your vram, resulting it in crap performance before you reloaded the textures. Not a huge deal but annoying.

I sometimes wish Steam had a middle of the road option for reviewing games because while Sniper Elite 5 isn't a terrible game, it's clearly a downgrade in what made Sniper Elite 4 very fun. Allow me to explain.

Sniper Elite 5 takes pride in itself in a few ways. One such pride is with its campaign's maps being very large. They are very welcoming to exploration and in a sense, adventure. There is no pressure against the player, you aren't timed as you move around, allowing to find all the little nooks and crannies as you move through these maps. Depending on the difficulty you want to play on, the game can easily make you feel pressured though, but that is entirely up to you in the end. So what's the problem then?

The major flaw with SE5 is its "expanded sandbox experience". While on first glance, it seems pretty welcoming with how you can approach enemies and dealing with them. It as a whole is a huge downgrade in interaction. An example of this is how Karl can knock out enemies, while neat and an interesting way to play pacifist, it becomes a double edged sword when a single guard you happened to miss wanders about and discovered the knocked out buddy and wakes him back up. But hey, there is a way to prevent this and keep your pacifist way right? Well there are those yellow supply chest, seemingly inspired by Hitman where you can store up to two enemies in them to effectively keep them out of the fight for the remaining part of your mission. There is also the tall grass too, which works just as well funny enough.

But the issue isn't how Karl takes down enemies in pacifistic way, its how he approaches them lethally. One of the huge flaws in this game which confused me was how the player approaches enemies in a more lethal sniper format. Now you can just point and click on the head, sure, but in the previous games you had the ability to target a grenade on an enemy's uniform or belt, causing it to explode, creating a distraction as well as panic among enemies. 90% of enemies in this game don't have grenades physically equipped to their belts anymore which is odd since they throw them like candy when they do spot you. 

Another large downgrade is the approach to vehicle combat, in this game weapon customization is a very strong boon the player has and the ability to make a suppressed anti-armor rifle is pretty neat, but the interaction between vehicles and the player is extremely limited. The very first level, Atlantikwall introduces you to vehicle patrols right after you complete the tutorial piece of the game and again, at first its pretty neat seeing a traveling patrol of trucks, wagens and bikes roaming around the maps (until it breaks, I'll get that towards the end of the review), but targeting of vehicle weakpoints is extremely hit or miss in SE5, even with Anti-Armor ammo, sometimes it takes up to two, four shots before you blow up a troop truck, even a wagen. Later in the same level, you encounter the first major flaw of this issue, the patrol boat. On the water in front of the beach bunkers is a boat with spotlight and turret.

In previous games, you could target the driver AND gunner of the boat, but in SE5 only the spotlight can be broken and the driver can be killed. The gunner can't be targeted at all and even looking at the gunner position reveals there is no visible soldier there, just a rotating empty combat position with a gun that seems to be alive on its own or operating via remote control. Its weird. Same thing applies to the Armored Car, the Sd. Kfz 222, its driver can be killed but for some reason, unlike SE4, the gunner can't be targeted at all. The same can be said of the Tiger II tank enemy where you can't even kill the driver or gunner. Its just a strange and odd choice of sandbox limitations given how "expanded" its suppose to be.

But now that I got my personal gripes out of the way, lets talk about the real reason why you should only buy it if you just want to play Sniper Elite. The bugs and the DLC consumer model. Oh golly. The bugs in this game are extremely visible and from what I've noticed, there has been little to zero attempt to fix them. In my 100+ hours of play, I've seen so many strange and odd bugs regarding the sandbox and how the AI interacts with it. Again, jump back to the first level, Atlantikwall again. One of the secondary objectives is blowing up a series of three Flak 38 emplacements (fun fact two enemies incorrectly call the 38s, 88s in their dialogue for some reason, another oddity moment), now its pretty straightforward, you blow up the first one and the second one without issue, its the last one by the Naval Cannon objective that breaks the game's sandbox. Upon blowing up that AA gun, enemies by the nearby road will come over to investigate and even some vehicle patrols will stop, hop out and investigate as well, but that's the issue. They will never stop investigating, leaving on your mini-map a strangely permanent mark of investigation. Even after all the enemies are dead or knocked out, it will not remove the mark.

This causes so many issues, no matter how far away you are. Enemies will stop reacting to your Whistle tool and reset their pathing, throwing a Bottle will aggro any enemies on the spot regardless if you are across the way, they'll know where you are at and open fire on your exact position. Vehicle pathing breaks as vehicles will stop in strange spots, get stuck and remain like this. The whole thing just breaks entirely and this happens on every single map. Its a "sandbox" problem and just from a glance, it seems be literally the AI unable to restore itself back to a normal pattern. It gets stuck, completely flubbing up how your mission flows as a result. Its bizarre.

Now then, the other reason why you should be wary. The DLC consumer model. Its bad. Its really bad. 10$ for a weapon and skin pack? 15$ for a single mission and weapon pack? It really screams money grubbing given the fact the maps are weirdly smaller and more compact compared to the base game content. The ONLY pack that is actually worth the 10$ is Kraken Awakens, given that its mission is placed on a decently big map and it properly wraps up the final strings on the campaign's story.

But what about the shooting funny mustache man DLC (Wolf Mountain DLC)? My disappoint is extreme and very depressing, this is one of the most bugged things I've ever seen. While the map is not as large as others, it has a lot of flow problems (ie, only one way to get to the main structure, through the tunnel where vehicle patrols come through commonly as example). On top of that Mr. H's AI is extremely broken. For some reason 90% of the game, he'll be standing in the open (spawned there) or just in sitting in his staff car not moving or doing anything. His bike escorts also seemingly stuck in place too (after peeking under the game's hood, it seems his front bike escort driver isn't even loaded properly most of the time; usually characters assigned to a mission have a set name and a bio. The rear bike escort does have this and on rare moments when the mission actually works, the front bike driver ALSO has a set name and bio, but if the driver is listed as "Unknown Soldier" aka a temporary soldier spawned in for vehicle patrolling, the mission breaks entirely; this is your reason right here). The fact that there was never a bug fix or addressing of this issue should tell you a lot about SE5 and its problems. There are other things but for me, gameplay and just general flow are my major points of frustration.

In the end however, it's a decently good game marred by a lot of issues and a lot more bugs. A lot of questionable downgrades as well, but I do find myself enjoying the whole sneaking around the maps, and self imposed challenges I gave myself as I play it. Regardless, its one of those games where you should think about before you buy. If you do wanna play it, I'd suggest waiting for a sale.

As an unconditional fan of the Sniper Elite franchise, I must analyze the fifth installment, which undoubtedly has its highs and lows.

To begin with, this fifth installment is essentially identical to the fourth in terms of mission structure and gameplay formula. This is generally not a bad thing, since, gameplay-wise, Sniper Elite 4 is a very good game. Possibly, one of the few aspects I liked the most is the atmosphere and the well-crafted levels.

And here comes the negative part. Rebellion, the developer, has brought us the same story for the third time: We are in the area, we investigate a Nazi superweapon, we destroy it, and finally we kill the mastermind behind it all. I know for many the story isn't important, but the same premise is getting tiresome.

Regarding enemies, we basically have the same as in the fourth, but without the Italian troops, so we basically see the same troops throughout the entire game. Possibly the worst aspect I see in this game is the weapons, since the base game includes very few. As an example of this lack of variety, we didn't even have a secondary shotgun, which was added later as free DLC. A rifle like the Lee Enfield was also added as free DLC, but weapons like the Mosin Nagant, the PPSh, the Mauser C96 pistol, or the Grease submachine gun are behind a paywall—weapons that were in the base game of previous installments.

But the worst part is that these weapons were already made in Zombie Army 4, a game that came out a year earlier and uses the same graphics engine as Sniper Elite 5. Basically, they copied and pasted them and are selling them separately. However, this problematic DLC issue has been evident since the third installment.

The question is, do I recommend Sniper Elite 5? If you liked the fourth installment, I recommend this one, but only when it's on sale, especially now that the price has dropped quite a bit with the latest discounts.

This version of the game is a solid improvement from the last one. Maps feels way more open, giving you more room to explore and play your way. Feel of distance is somehow better. Objects look far away when they should.
The graphics are seriously impressive—everything looks cleaner and more detailed. Enemies are trickier to spot now, which adds a nice layer of challenge. 
Overall, it's just a more polished and immersive experience.

After 5+ hours on Sniper Elite difficulty (Chapters 1-2), here’s my take: This game nails realism. Yeah, salty folks whine 'AC-style knives > sniping!' — but that’s the point! Suppressors muffle shots; they don’t make you invisible. Enemies should swarm your last known position. Silent knife kills? Possible, but suppressed guns still trigger searches (unless extreme-range). No 'ghost sniper' BS where you camp one spot slaughtering fish in a barrel. The thrill? Tactical repositioning after every shot. That’s authentic, balls-to-the-wall tension. Major flaw? DLCs are overpriced AF — short content, zero value. Wait for a sale; skip full price.

It's just good enough to pass. But barely. Still good enough to keep me playing, slowly, for dozens of hours, so it's doing something right...

- The story is bland (solo agent singlehandedly penetrates Nazi strongholds and disables a WMD).
But... It holds things together.

- The freedom is annoyingly restricted - maps are just patches of gameplay in a LARGE map, but connected by narrow paths that artificially confine player movement. It's annoying that a small hedge holds you back, and you can't climb in/out trenches, and you cannot jump... Not at all. So many things look entirely traversable but aren't.
But... You get used to it, and at least you can *shoot* all across the map. Which you sometimes need to do, and albeit artificial, it keeps you from too much running & gunning (at least on higher levels because you die easily).

- They say the sniping is "authentic"... But you just press "space" and a useful diamond comes up that assists in headshot after headshot even at extremely long distances. And there is x-ray vision for enemies you saw once, which makes it incredibly easy to plan a route and stay undetected, just as long as you have patience.
But... Yeah, shooting is fun.

- The enemy AI is one of the most braindead AI's ever in a game like this. They see five of their buddies getting headshotted in a building doorway, and they think "hey, maybe if I walk through the door as well, I catch the sniper, hey you know what? let me LOUDLY yell ahead that I'm coming through as well". It's ridiculous. They are alone, and they loudly yell to their imaginary friend or to me, the sniper, just to let me know they're there, so I can take them down with great ease. They don't listen, they don't look around, they don't work together, they don't take cover, they don't change weapons, they don't take strategic positions, they don't create funnels, they don't draw me out of a hiding place (except from the odd grenade), they don't cover each other, they don't care at all about their wounded buddies, they glitch and look/shoot through doors and walls...
But... No, there's no but for this one. The insanely terrible AI is, for me, by far the hardest hit on the immersion, and made me ragequit often.

But the maps are gorgeous and large, and the environments (especially the indoors) are detailed, chaotic and very well done. Even if traversing chokepoints is often extremely artificial and limiting. It's fun mowing down countless numbers of bad guys in a combination of slowly scouting from the edges of the map, and then barging in and having hectic firefights in maze-like indoors quarters, churches, science stations, armories etc..

I'm not military, so I have no idea if this is is anything like sniping at all, but "authentic sniping"? Nah, absolutely, definitely not even close.

Sniper Elite 5 is a third person shooter set during World War 2, where player character Karl Fairburne is sent on another mission to stop a top secret Nazi weapons project being developed in France.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

•	Missions take place in ruined cities, rural towns, and fortified German strongholds. Each location is quite large and contains multiple main and secondary objectives. There are usually a few different paths to move around each map.

•	You can equip a sniper rifle, SMG, and pistol. There are several different types of each weapon to unlock, and most of the ones I tried felt pretty good to use.

•	Each weapon can be customised with mods which are unlocked by finding workbenches hidden around each map. You can adjust stats such as damage, rate of fire, clip size, recoil, noise range, and reload speed. 

•	You can also carry various useful items such as medkits, grenades and mines. In addition to defending narrow chokepoints and doorways, one of my favourite uses for explosives was to booby trap corpses of enemy soldiers so that when someone else came to investigate, I’d eliminate them too.

•	Most enemies are equipped with the same pistols, SMGs and rifles that the player can use. You’ll also encounter a few armoured cars and tanks, so be on the lookout for panzerfaust RPGs.

•	There are a few ways to take advantage of stealth, including silenced weapons and sneaking up behind enemies for melee takedowns. You can whistle and throw bottles to cause nearby enemies to investigate the noise. And if there are loud environmental noises such as planes flying overhead, or cannons firing, this can mask the sound of your rifle fire. However, each map has a large number of enemies, and they can see you over quite a long distance, so I found it hard to stay hidden for long. 

•	When alerted to your presence, the AI will quickly identify your location and aggressively chase you, usually with multiple soldiers from different directions. Objective locations often have alarms which will summon more reinforcements until you disable the alarm. During a couple of missions I had lengthy and very chaotic firefights against massive numbers of enemies.

•	I played on the hard difficulty and while I died a few times on each mission, it was rarely frustrating. Most of my deaths resulted from attempting to be stealthy and messing up in an exposed location. When I started just shooting everyone on sight from a more tactically secure location, it actually became much easier.

[h1]Story[/h1]

•	The writing and voice acting are both average quality. The story only really exists to give you a reason to perform each mission objective.

•	The story doesn’t connect to the previous games in any significant way, so if you haven’t played the other games you wouldn’t feel like you’re missing anything.

[h1]Technical[/h1]

•	It took me 14 hours to complete the campaign and I only missed 2 optional objectives. There’s also a survival mode where you have to fight multiple waves of enemies while defending a control point, which could provide a few more hours of playtime.

•	Controls are fully rebindable and work great with mouse and keyboard.

•	I didn’t have any crashes or framerate problems.

•	I noticed a frequent flicker/shimmer effect on distant objects like trees and narrow railings, which I think might be caused by poor anti-aliasing. You can’t choose which type to use, you can only select low/medium/high/ultra, which didn’t seem to make any difference.

•	There is some inconsistency relating to whether or not you can climb over walls and other waist high objects. Sometimes I approached an object that my eyes told me should be climbable, but the game wouldn’t let me interact with it.

[h1]Recommendation[/h1]

Sniper Elite 5 is a good game that has fun and challenging combat, but is let down slightly by average storytelling and a couple of technical issues. I think most action game fans will probably enjoy the game.

1. This is doubly baffling as to why it was removed as this was one feature Sniper Elite IV was praised for being "ahead of it's time".

2. 3. Replacement of Infinite Stones with Finite Bottles: This is a particular bug-bare of mine as in previous Sniper Elite games you could cheese the entire games on any difficulty by luring away every German one at a time, this took hours though and was more a fault with the AI being too thick to realise that their battalion strength unit had mysteriously disappeared in the past couple of hours... This also completely ruins a secondary use for Stones, which was to destroy light sources, you can still do that with bottles... but for the fact that you only carry a base amount of FOUR. Meaning that if you want to destroy lighting to aid with your stealth you have to use bullets (great) instead or spend hours running back to pick up more bottles. This is like when they replaced Heat Sinks with Thermal Clips Between Mass Effect 1 & 2, it made no sense lore wise but was implemented to make the game less individual and more like every other third person cover shooter. 

4. Contrived map design & Invisible walls: This is quite possibly the worst area in which SE5 is a downgrade from SE4, despite having huge maps, instead of being large open sandbox typed areas everywhere instead seems like an extremely contrived series of arenas, invisible walls in the forms of low wall barriers, that for inexplicable reasons the player is unable to vault over, obvious cover and flanking points, like every area was purposefully designed for a Sniper's convenience. Sure SE4 did this somewhat too, yet the environments felt more like real world places, with more options open for the player to use their own initiative in completing objectives. Every map I have played so far just feels like a Sniper Elite 3 map on a larger scale. 

5. Invisible magnets: When enemies are alerted to you, by firing your gun or what not they will frequently fly into cover as if they are a big lump of metal being snapped into position by a large magnet. This also happens with the Player too when moving into cover and is perhaps one of the worse faults with this game as it can and will mess up your shots, picture this, you're in empty lung and are just waiting for an enemy soldier to run into your line of fire only for you to pull the trigger and the invisible hand of god to move them two meters to the left behind a wall in a fraction of a second. This will happen every time you try to kill more than one person in Empty Lung at a time.

I was getting far more kills in Authentic in SE5 than I would do in SE4 playing without the Aim Assist.

7. Silenced Pistol pre-order bonus is only available for Axis snipers in Invasion mode. Self explanatory.

8. Hangovers from Multiplayer in Singleplayer: I don't know how universal this is, but I got really excited the first time I entered a Bunker on the first mission and saw a phone on the wall that said "Invasion only", my immediate thought was that if either I or the AI picked up that phone it would alert all of the Germans on the map to the Allied invasion of Normandy.. what a cool feature I thought, distracting all of the enemies from one side of the map whilst I sneak in the back. it took me a couple of seconds to realise that no, it's some multiplayer bullshit that has been left in the Singleplayer despite having "Invasion mode" disabled. If it's disabled it shouldn't be there, I've no idea what the stupid phone does and I'll never find out as the day I enable Invasion mode is the day I decide to swap my PC for a Mac. 

9. Lame Aesthetic: The Aesthetic of the previous games, the cute tutorial cards, the atmosphere, the UI, the HUD, the menus, it's all been stripped out, the game now looks like a generic multiplayer shooter with all of the little artistic qwerks and style sucked out of it giving a bland appearance.

To Rebellions in House BLM representation and equality adviser: Whilst there is no problem whatsoever with having Black playable characters in game, I find myself really really really having to stretch my imagination to believe that a Black SOE agent, a Black French Resistance Fighter and Black soldier of the Segregated 555th Airborne (a unit which never did active service in Western Europe, or anywhere outside the Continental United States for that matter during the war) have any place in a WW2 game set in North Western France during D-Day. It's less believable than the Nazi Super McGuffins that Rebellion comes up with every game, it breaks immersion though honestly the real issue with this is that it ignores the Racial Prejudices that were common amongst the Allied nations of the time and creates a false impression that people of colour were treated the same as Europeans, which they weren't by any European army/society of the time, indeed it trivialises the actual race struggles that took place. Don't get me wrong though the Axis side isn't portrayed any better, it portrays all of the Nazi's as being Germans when in actuality, many of those serving in North Western France during this time period were "Ost Regiments", that is Russians, Eastern Europeans, even Indians served in the SS on the Atlantic Wall. As the game is right now having any actual knowledge of history is a hindrance to enjoying the game.

## 🎯 Single Player  
The base campaign maps (without DLC) look great – big, detailed, and atmospheric. Some areas are perfect for stealth, but I often wish there were more opportunities for true long-range sniping. The level design is impressive, but replaying missions quickly becomes repetitive.  

For achievement hunters, it can be exhausting. A good example is the “Wolf Mountain” mission with Hitler – killing him in a dozen different ways just to unlock achievements feels like filler content. It adds hours of repetition without much creativity from the developers.  

I’ve logged around 350 hours in the game, and while the campaign is enjoyable, replay fatigue is definitely real.  

---

## ⚔️ Axis Invasion  
Axis Invasion is probably the most exciting addition to Sniper Elite 5. Dropping in as a Jäger sniper to hunt down another player completely changes the atmosphere of the campaign. It’s tense, unpredictable, and often thrilling.  

Unfortunately, this mode suffers from serious balance issues – usually against the invader:  
- You can’t loot fallen soldiers for extra weapons, traps, or grenades. You’re stuck with two grenades, a mine, and a medkit.  
- The invaded player has big advantages: looting gear, using phones to track you, and even seeing hints of where you’re approaching from.  
- Worst of all, “Sniper Focus” feels like an unfair advantage – allowing the invaded player to see your location through walls and prepare an ambush.  

Camping makes it worse. Many players clear the entire map of AI, plant mines everywhere, and then sit in a high spot (like a church tower) with perfect vision. Most of my deaths as an invader were simply from running into yet another mine.  

AI isn’t helpful either. If enemies are shooting at the campaign player, I should get an exact location update. Footstep sounds are also too quiet, making sound-based tracking unreliable.  

---

## 🛡️ Survival  
Survival mode is fun, but it highlights a big flaw across the game: there’s no proper tutorial explaining mechanics, scoring, or what actions give the most points. You have to figure it all out yourself.  

Difficulty scaling is also frustrating. Getting a gold medal feels almost impossible on lower difficulties like *Civilian* or *Very Easy*. Maps are sometimes designed to overwhelm you with enemies from all sides, leaving no chance to respond. The mode is intense, but it lacks balance.  

---

## 🔫 Multiplayer  
I’ve only played a few dozen matches, but the main issue is clear: **everything requires grinding**.  
- You unlock weapon attachments in the campaign, but then you must unlock them again in Axis Invasion.  
- In Survival, you also need unlocks, or you’re stuck with bare-bones gear.  
- In Multiplayer, you have to grind all the way to level 50 to access the full arsenal.  

This system feels unfair – new players are stuck with basic weapons, long aim times, and no attachments, while higher-level players dominate. On top of that, there’s a “Prestige” system where you re-grind levels from scratch for small perks. Honestly, it feels lazy.  

Other issues:  
- **Easy Anti-Cheat** doesn’t seem to stop cheaters, but it does eat resources, cause micro-stutters, and add lag.  
- The **wheel menu** is clunky. In combat, it blocks the screen and wastes time. Hotkeys for ammo and explosives would’ve been better.  
- **Weapon customization** is excellent, but loadouts reset across game modes. And you can’t name custom loadouts, which makes things confusing.  

---

## ✅ Pros  
- Beautiful maps and textures  
- Axis Invasion is exciting and unique  
- Wide choice of sniper rifles and secondary weapons  
- Deep and satisfying weapon customization  

## ❌ Cons  
- Repetitiveness kills replay value  
- Poor balance in Axis Invasion  
- Too much grinding across every mode  
- Easy Anti-Cheat hurts performance  
- Wheel menu slows gameplay  
- Lack of realism in animations, physics, and AI  

---

## 📝 Final Thoughts  
Sniper Elite 5 is a good game – even a very good one in some areas – with beautiful visuals, strong sniping mechanics, and a brilliant idea in Axis Invasion. But it also feels unfinished, with too much grinding, weak AI, and mechanics that often frustrate more than they entertain.  

For me, Sniper Elite 2 / Sniper Elite V2 Remastered still holds the crown for the most satisfying overall experience. Sniper Elite 5 is revolutionary in parts, but disappointing in others.  

My advice? Wait for a good sale, grab the Season Pass bundles, and give it a try. It’s worth playing – just be ready for grind, bugs, and missed opportunities.

Is it strange to call [i]Sniper Elite 5[/i] ("SE5") a beautiful game, unironically? Like, subject matter aside, shooting a dude in the testicles is objectively gross, especially when you hear a squelch and see a human skeleton. I dunno, I guess I have a weak stomach. But, like, SE5 is a beautiful game. I don't mean the graphics, though, but [i]wow[/i] is the game gorgeous. I mean how it lets you move through and interact with its environments. The added movement mechanics, gunplay, customization, and, most importantly, the maps themselves make SE5 feel like more than just a game about going somewhere and shooting everyone.

And, yeah, killing Nazis is always fun.

[b][h2]Pros:[/h2][/b]
✅ [b]Being a sniper.[/b] As I mentioned in my intro, there are moments when you find a good sniping perch, look through your scope, and suddenly the entire map opens up. You can see patrols moving through the streets, vehicles coming and going, enemies stationed in buildings, and all the little routes and opportunities you hadn't noticed on the ground. There's no timer. You can take as long as you want to angle the scope juuust right, waiting for a soldier to pace back and forth while you listen to birds chirping or tanks rumbling. You can [i]see[/i] how plentiful the map is, but sometimes it feels like just you against the world.

✅ [b]More fluid movement.[/b] I played [i]Sniper Elite 4[/i] on Nintendo Switch a while ago, so I can't quite remember whether these mechanics were present then. If they were, ignore me! But I loved the added physicality to SE5. Karl can now jump, crawl, climb, shimmy, and hang from ledges, pipes, or vines, and slide down ziplines. It's just [i]so[/i] freeing how you can approach a building from the front, sneak around the back, climb up to a window, or find some ridiculous little crawlspace. 

✅ [b]Customization[/b]. I really like how much control SE5 gives you over your weapons. You can modify your rifle, scope, suppressor, magazine, stock, and a shit ton of other parts, so you can build your loadout around how you want to play. Do you want something quieter? More accurate? Faster to reload? Better at long range? There are trade-offs, so it doesn't feel like you're just constantly replacing your gun with a bigger number. A bolt-action sniper, for instance, handles differently from a semi-automatic sniper rifle. 

✅ [b]Maps.[/b] Honestly, the maps are probably my favorite thing about SE5. They're big, detailed, and full of little paths, buildings, interiors, rooftops, courtyards, tunnels, vehicles, and environmental opportunities. They range from a towering chateau to an intimate war-torn battlefield to an idyllic countryside. More importantly, however, they don't feel like they're designed around one single solution. You can spend ten minutes planning how you'll infiltrate an area, then completely abandon that plan when you notice a window, a conveniently placed explosive, a tunnel, a padlocked door, or a patrol route you can exploit. So many little details make exploration worthwhile, and I constantly found myself stopping to look around and figure out exactly [i]how[/i] many entrances could get me into this damned castle. Like, these maps take a [i]while[/i] to clear, ranging anywhere from two to five hours. Dare I say, SE5 is a bit immersive sim-like?

✅ [b]Flexible difficulty.[/b] Surprisingly, you can tweak pretty much every difficulty setting. Authentic difficulty—the highest—isn't just "enemy health goes up." Nah. You'll pay much more attention to your positioning, timing, sound, enemy awareness, and ballistics. Not to mention the HUD, enemy aggression, health regeneration, damage taken, and more! Suddenly that perfect shot isn't just "line up the crosshair and click." You have to actually think about distance, movement, wind, and whether taking the shot is even worth revealing your position. 

✅ [b]Collectibles.[/b] Normally, I tolerate collectibles because the game tells me I should. SE5 actually made me want to look for them. There are a couple of types. One is Stone Eagles, little statues usually hidden at a map's highest point. It requires a good eye and aim to hit them. Another type is letters or notes, which contain information that unlocks new objectives, cool lore, or funny stories. My favorite, though, are the little soldier blurbs you get when you "tag" an enemy with your bincolours. They're pretty short, maybe a sentence or two, but they manage to convey the whole range of human emotions.

[b][h2]Cons:[/h2][/b]
🟥 [b]Some achievements require multiplayer.[/b]

🟥 [b]Some bugs.[/b] Nothing that completely ruined the game for me, but SE5 definitely has its moments. Enemies can occasionally get stuck running into a wall or on a rock, animations can get a little wonky, and I've had a moment where the in-game achievements thought I got two stars on a mission instead of three.

🟥 [b]I don't looooove the two season passes and DLC-locked missions and guns, but I guess that's just the era we live in now.[/b]

As a player with over 1,700 hours in SE4 and completed SEV2 and SE3, I feel pretty letdown so far. I only play on Authentic. I REALLY want to like this game. But after playing a few more hours, it appears that Rebellion has jumped the shark with this release.

1. There is no wind on the majority of the game I have played, eliminating the challenge of compensating for that. You would have figured they could have at least put in some significant winds when you are on the coastline literally staring at the English Channel. The shooting mechanics have now become unskilled center of crosshair shooting. The wind feels so non-existent from my gameplay that I've been actually questioning if it's a bug. Yes, I get that it was exaggerated in SE4 / SE3 / SEV2, but that made it fun and differentiated the rifles and muzzle velocities, and gave an additional acquired skill factor. You no longer really have to zero a rifle, because it doesn't matter. I don't even look at the wind indicator anymore because it doesn't move 98% of the time. It doesn't feel like a sniping game anymore.
2. The bullet trails coming off enemies bullets look like jumbo jet contrails. I would have thought they could be toned down or removed in Authentic.
3. As others have mentioned, I do not know why they went in the misguided direction of all the non-lethal stuff.
4. I liked the movement of SE4 better. SE5 feels clumsier, almost reminiscent of the clumsiness that SE3 felt like.
5. The coop survival mode camaraderie of reviving people now takes a turn for the worse due to needing medkits to revive your teammates. So all you can do is watch them go down and die if you don't have any to spare. And of course if you use them on a teammate, you no longer have them to heal yourself.
6. In coop survival, ammo at command posts can now be challenging to share. One person can walk up to the command post after a wave has started and basically take it all, leaving no ammo for teammates. That is going to case a lot of tension, and also be a camaraderie breaker.
7. The white outline around your character while your character is in foliage in Authentic is tacky looking and really takes away from the experience of actually feeling like you are hidden in a bush.
8. When you are playing survival, even in Authentic, they put white outlines around the last 5 guys. Seriously, training wheel kid shit like that shouldn't be in Authentic.
9. There aren't many snipers in coop survival, and it looks like the positions of them aren't going to vary much. They also seem to be less of a threat than the snipers on SE4.
10. The AI is completely brain-dead. Often, you'll find guys just sitting there inexplicably while a complete gunfight is going on. Their reaction time is slow, and you can just run at them and melee then before they even think about shooting at you.

Hopefully things like these get adjusted in patches, SE5 has been two or three steps back from what they had going in SE4. It's hard to determine if they are trying to only appeal to the casual gamer that just wants to run through the game like it's a movie and dumbed down the skill level to remedial levels for them.

Rebellion dumbed down the difficulty of SE5 bigtime by pretty much removing bullet wind mechanics, and making the AI clueless in comparison to previous SE games. So unless they address major things like that, the game might indeed just be plain boring. It's so far off from being fun in the skill regard that I don't even know if they'll be able to salvage it with patches. Most of the die hard regular SE4 players that I know feel that way. And that comes from someone who has played over 1700 hours of SE4 and REALLY wanted to love SE5.

I initially gave this game 3 out of 5 stars but after playing for several hours I decided to change my review to 5 out of 5 stars. I just needed some time to adjust to a couple of changes they made in this new game. It's a fun game.

Short Version:
This game is a heavily watered down experience compared to previous entries. If you are looking at getting into Sniper Elite as a franchise do not start with this. Start with V2, 3, or 4. They only get better as you go on from V2. I really hope they cook hard for Sniper Elite 6 when/if it comes out. This game is a pretty heavy departure in style from the previous entries and that is, in my opinion, to it's detriment.

Long Version:
This game feels like an overall regression for the series. 

The 5 biggest issues are:

1. Map Size/Enemy Population
2. Overall Level Design (and lack of sniping as a result)
3. Mechanical Regression (items, movement, etc.)
4. Non-Lethal Options
5. Extremely lacking difficulty options

The maps are far too big with far too little enemies. I found myself out loud questioning "only X number of guards here?" or "where are the enemies?" during missions. I'm to believe this is the height of the occupation of France during WW2 but it feels like the Germans just left some stragglers behind for me to pick off. This severely hampers the experience even on the hardest difficulties and ruins believability of the setting. Many have thrown around that this is to improve the performance on previous gen consoles. Screw previous gen consoles, maps should not be 150% the size of Sniper Elite 4's maps with 50% of it's population. And they also boasted that the maps are recreations of real life locations in France, which leads into my next point...

The level design has regressed. There are really only two standout maps, and all the rest feel worse than Sniper Elite 4 and even Sniper Elite 3. V2 can't really be compared with it's very linear nature. The maps were "faithful recreations" of real French locations during occupation. This does not mean they function well as video game levels. There are tons of invisible walls, random blocks to seemingly clear routes, and terrain that looks to be climbable but isn't for some reason. They had the formula down for the previous entry, where you make a good level first and then make it looks like it could really exists afterwards. The main detriment of all of this is the severe lack of long range sniping in most levels. The previous games had strong sniping positions (often called Sniper Nests or power positions) all throughout the levels with clear sight lines and advantages like sound masking and cover. This game has some but they very rarely give you good sight lines or just straight up block half the map with trees and bushes to prevent you from getting more than maybe 4 or 5 kills. This forces very pistol/secondary-heavy close range gameplay which really should not be the focus. 

In that same vein the mechanical complexity just feels dumbed down. Weapon customization is cool, map tools like bolt cutters and crowbars are neat, and new ammo types are fun, But they also removed a lot. Various mines were removed, rocks were replaced with inferior bottles, the skill point system is very dumb, and the biggest downgrade is movement. Movement feels clunkier, and I don't know how they did it but maybe it's the engine? Button prompts are often delayed when interacting with things, the player character frequently gets out of sneak mode when interacting or finishing interacting with thing, and they removed crouch sprinting. Why would you remove the ability to sneak a bit faster when your maps are 150% bigger. I know it sounds like a nitpick but it's such a downgrade in practical gameplay. Also binocular tagging is just annoying now, where instead of clicking what you want to tag you have to hold over it for a little bit. This is annoying and results in both accidental tags, which you can't remove unlike previous games, and constant missed tags. It used to be if I sniped an officer I could mark his corpse to find later for that sweet Duty Roster, but don't worry they also removed Duty Rosters too. I don't care about the invasion mode they added. I'm not about PVP, nor about harming people trying to do single player content. And I am ESPECIALLY not about playing as a Nazi. I play these games to kill Nazis, not be one. Speaking of which...

They added non-lethal options. This should be self explanatory. Your enemies are Nazis. I don't care if they have funny little info popups when you tag them, or if they're humans just like you and me. They are Nazis. I don't think there is a more universal enemy possible, it's practically family friendly fun to kill them. This is not Metal Gear Solid, you are not gonna be haunted by ghosts or grow devil horns. They are Nazis, kill them. Schu mines are dumb, wooden bullets are ESPECIALLY dumb, and when enemies are injured and laying on the ground dying of blood loss they should "BLEED OUT" like every previous entry and not be "INCAPACITATED" like in this one. Don't gimme a chart at the end and act like I'm a good little sniper for "sparing" some enemies on the map. If I saw em, if I knew they were breathing, I'd have killed them without a second damn thought. Kill Nazis. End of story. 

Lastly this is a minor point for me personally, but some dedicated members of the community really care about it. Difficulty options are lacking compared to previous entries. Beyond having too few enemies they are also less diverse and less difficult. And they also removed Authentic Plus. Why? I don't personally do super hard challenges, but for the significant part of the community that does this is a major detriment. Authentic overall is much easier too according to said part of the community. Bring it back or at least add custom difficulty sliders for people. 

Overall, if you want to get into this series please don't start with this one. I really tried my best to like this game, and it's still *fine* as a game, but when compared to it's predecessors it falls flat. If you still want to try it for yourself please get it at a discount somehow.

Being German myself, I'd like to comment on the design of the Germans in the game.

The first thing is the language and voice acting. It's great that German soldiers speak native German, but the actual acting is horrible. There are also literal translations from English expressions in their lines, that aren't proper German, as well as smaller details, like grammar errors in Propaganda Posters.
I know the game had expert advisors on weapons and such, why couldn't they have also had just one or two German people to check for this kind of thing? They would have spotted all of it immediately.

The level design goes for oversimplified Pseudo-German set pieces, like a large sign that just says "Achtung!" in the middle of a camp. I get that this is useful for being recognizable by Non-Germans, but that sign makes no sense. "Achtung!" for what? There needs to be some explanation on what that sign is a warning against. Especially since German is famous for being very detailed and specific.

I don't want to make this too long, so I'll say this in conclusion. In order for me to enjoy fighting enemies in a game, I have to be able to take them seriously and have respect for them. That is what is lacking here. Even though my complaints may be less problematic for Non-Germans, I'm certain that a more authentic depiction of them would make for a much better game for everyone.

So please, pay more attention ("Achtung!") to detail when designing villains, antagonists and enemies.
